title: How Ouija Boards Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how Ouija boards work, starting with the pre-game banter about moving offices and a planned seance. They cover the board's history: earlier divination and talking boards, the spiritualism movement of the 19th century, Elijah Bond's patent and rival Swastika board, Charles Kennard and William Fuld, and Parker Brothers/Hasbro. They describe the board and planchette, how to use it, and the ideomotor effect (Carpenter, Chevreul's pendulum, the ring-on-a-string gender test). They also discuss facilitated communication as a related controversy. They close with anecdotes (the Kansas City Herbert and Nellie Herd case, the El Cerrito mass hysteria, Sax Rohmer's Fu Manchu), a blindfold test suggestion, and listener mail about a crack baby.

segments.title: Opening banter and Ouija board history
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the office move and a planned seance, then discuss the Ouija name, The Exorcist, and the board's origins as a mass-marketed Parker Brothers game.

segments.title: Pre-19th century divination and spiritualism
segments.summary: They note the board itself is likely no older than the mid-19th century and American in origin, while earlier divination used pendulums and alphabet discs. They tie it to the spiritualism movement and seances, with mediums often female.

segments.title: Dial plate, alphabet board, and planchette
segments.summary: Earlier talking devices included the dial plate, the alphabet board, and the planchette, a heart-shaped board on three legs with a pencil that could write messages.

segments.title: Patents, ownership, and rival boards
segments.summary: Elijah Bond improved an existing patent, sold rights to Charles Kennard, then made a rival swastika-branded board through his West Virginia company. William Fuld ran with marketing and stamped his name as inventor; the name story is discussed. The board passed to Parker Brothers and later Hasbro.

segments.title: Board design and how to use it
segments.summary: The board's design is described: alphabet, numbers, yes and no corners, and goodbye. The instructions call for two or more players with fingertips on the planchette, asking questions aloud, and ending with goodbye. Tips include concentration, dim lights, and avoiding scary questions.

segments.title: Ideomotor effect and the science of movement
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the planchette moves through unconscious muscle movement, the ideomotor effect named by William Carpenter. Chevreul's pendulum and the gender ring test illustrate it. Facilitated communication is also raised as a related controversy.

segments.title: Ouija board anecdotes and a home test
segments.summary: Stories include a Kansas City case where a board message led to a fatal dispute, an El Cerrito, California mass hysteria episode, and Sax Rohmer's claim that a board spelled out Fu Manchu's origin. A blindfold test is suggested for home experiments.

segments.title: Listener mail: crack baby
segments.summary: A listener from Austin, Texas, describes calming a crack-exposed newborn while volunteering at a children's hospital around 2001.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener stories and direct listeners to the website and social accounts.
